title: ‘The clock on AI regulation is ticking’, warns UN rights chief
source_used: UN News story (https://news.un.org/en/story/2026/10/1168529), read in full from the main session's fetched text
key_facts: UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk spoke on Monday 5 Oct 2026 at an AI and Human Rights Summit in Oxford, UK.
He warned that the world is running out of time to put guardrails on AI as a 'ruthless race' between companies and countries raises concerns about human safety and even humanity's survival.
He said AI tools are built and controlled by a select few without public oversight and already do things their creators cannot fully predict or manage.

He warned AI could undermine equality, freedom, privacy and public debate, 'letting dystopia creep in unnoticed', and that populations could be cut off from communication, clean water, heating and financial services 'at the click of a button'.

He called for urgent action to prohibit machines from deciding who lives and who dies, and for mandatory human rights safeguards and due diligence; countries that host AI companies must require them to act responsibly.

He said some areas need new legal approaches but updating rules on liability, cybersecurity and data protection could protect people in the meantime, and urged stronger industry collaboration on security and independent monitoring.
He welcomed the UN's Global Dialogue on AI Governance and Independent International Scientific Panel on AI, and a joint call for tighter control of frontier AI models backed by 29 States and the EU.

UN News says his remark that industry leaders took new steps last week is apparently a reference to the voluntary White House accord of 29 Sep, which carries no penalties; he said 'Too few are walking the talk'.
quote_evidence: The world is running out of time to put guardrails on artificial intelligence, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk warned Monday, as a “ruthless race” between companies and countries raises concerns about human safety and even humanity’s survival.
He called for urgent action to prohibit machines from deciding who lives and who dies, noting that AI is already changing the face of warfare.
“Too few are walking the talk”, said the rights chief, who wrote to States and frontier AI companies three weeks ago urging them to act now to reduce risks.
why_it_matters_hint: The UN's top human rights official adds weight to calls for mandatory AI safeguards, but a speech sets no rule.
notes: UN News is the United Nations' own news service and reports on its own official, so no outside outlet was checked. The link to the 29 Sep White House accord is UN News's own reading ('apparently a reference'); kept hedged in the entry. The same article notes that New York City Council held a hearing on AI risks the same day (see C05-01).
